propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of IRCC Officer's decision rejecting permanent residency and finding inadmissibility for misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks judicial review of the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) Officer’s decision rejecting his application for permanent residency and finding him inadmissible for misrepresentation, pursuant to subsection 4(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [Regulations] and paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of IRCC Officer's decision rejecting permanent residency and finding inadmissibility for misrepresentation, court states.

propositions.text: Judicial review is dismissed; ineffective representation is not persuasive; key issue is marriage genuineness.
propositions.quote: For the reasons below, I am dismissing this judicial review. Even if I were persuaded, which I am not, that the Applicant had “ineffective” representation in the completion of his permanent residence application, the determinative issue on this judicial review is the finding that the marriage was not genuine.

propositions.text: Marriage genuineness finding based on inconsistencies and contradictory evidence from Applicant and spouse during interviews, unrelated to representative's competence.
propositions.quote: This finding was made based upon inconsistencies and contradictory evidence from the Applicant and his spouse during their interviews and is therefore unrelated to the quality or competence of the Applicant’s representative.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review, finds marriage genuineness issue based on inconsistent evidence, unrelated to representation quality.

propositions.text: Officer's misrepresentation finding was not solely based on failure to provide addresses and disclose US applications.
propositions.quote: I disagree with the Applicant’s claim that the Officer’s finding of misrepresentation was based solely on the failure of the Applicant, or his representative, to provide addresses and disclose his previous United States (US) applications.

propositions.text: Core issue for Officer was genuineness of the marriage, reading decision as a whole.
propositions.quote: Reading the decision as a whole, it is clear that the core issue for the Officer was the genuineness of the marriage.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer's misrepresentation finding focused on marriage genuineness, not just address or US application omissions.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh is Indian citizen applying for permanent residency under family class, sponsored by spouse Ms. Davidson.
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh is a citizen of India who applied for permanent residency in Canada under the family class category being sponsored by his spouse, Ms. Davidson.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh met Ms. Davidson Dec 19, 2022; married July 18, 2023; filed spousal sponsorship Nov 2023 using former representative Mr. D.
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh first met Ms. Davidson on December 19, 2022, and they married seven months later on July 18, 2023. In November 2023, they filed an application for spousal sponsorship and used Mr. Singh’s former immigration representative, whom I will refer to only as Mr. D.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Singh, Indian citizen, married Ms. Davidson and applied for spousal sponsorship using former representative Mr. D.

propositions.text: IRCC requested in-person interview April 29, 2024; Officer interviewed couple together and separately.
propositions.quote: On April 24, 2024, IRCC requested an in-person interview with the couple for April 29, 2024. On that date, the Officer interviewed Mr. Singh and Ms. Davidson together and separately.

propositions.text: Officer asked basic questions about each other; inconsistencies raised concern about marriage legitimacy.
propositions.quote: They were asked basic questions about each other, such as their educational background, their first meeting and wedding, and employment. Due to inconsistencies in their answers, the Officer expressed concern about the legitimacy of the marriage.

propositions.text: Officer gave Mr. Singh opportunity to address concerns including failure to disclose US visa rejections and address history.
propositions.quote: The Officer gave Mr. Singh the opportunity to address these concerns including his failure to disclose two US visa rejections and his complete address history in his permanent residency application.

paragraphs.summary: IRCC interviewed couple, found inconsistencies raising marriage legitimacy concerns, gave Mr. Singh chance to respond.

propositions.text: On April 30, 2024, Procedural Fairness Letter outlined concerns about marriage legitimacy and omissions in addresses and US visa refusals.
propositions.quote: Following the interview, on April 30, 2024, Mr. Singh was issued a Procedural Fairness Letter in which the Officer outlined concerns regarding the legitimacy of the marriage, based on inconsistencies between Mr. Singh’s and Ms. Davidson’s answers at the interview, communications history, and their lack of knowledge of each other. The letter also expressed concerns about omissions of Mr. Singh’s past addresses and refused US visa applications.

propositions.text: Letter requested response by May 7, 2024; Mr. Singh’s representative replied May 6, 2024.
propositions.quote: This letter requested that Mr. Singh respond to the stated concerns by May 7, 2024. On May 6, 2024, Mr. Singh’s representative sent a reply.

paragraphs.summary: Procedural Fairness Letter raised concerns about marriage and omissions, requested response; reply sent May 6, 2024.

propositions.text: Permanent residency application refused May 16, 2024, as marriage not genuine under subsection 4(1)(b) of Regulations.
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh received the decision, dated May 16, 2024, refusing his permanent residency application under subsection 4(1)(b) of the Regulations, because Mr. Singh was not in a genuine marriage with Ms. Davidson and therefore ineligible for permanent residency under the family class category.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision refused permanent residency May 16, 2024, finding marriage not genuine.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh found inadmissible for 5 years for material misrepresentation under subsection 40(1) IRPA.
propositions.quote: The decision also states that Mr. Singh was found inadmissible to Canada for 5 years for making a material misrepresentation, pursuant to subsection 40(1) of IRPA.

propositions.text: Misrepresentation involved failure to disclose Quebec addresses and two US visa rejections.
propositions.quote: Specifically, Mr. Singh had failed to disclose addresses that he had in Quebec, under which he made a refugee claim. Mr. Singh also failed to disclose two US visa rejections.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision found Mr. Singh inadmissible for 5 years for misrepresentation by nondisclosure of addresses and US visa refusals.

propositions.text: Issues raised: ineffective representation, reasonable apprehension of bias, breach of procedural fairness, and decision reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The Applicant raises the following issues: Did Mr. Singh have ineffective representation? Was there a reasonable apprehension of bias against the Officer? 3.Was there otherwise a breach of procedural fairness and natural justice? Is the decision reasonable?

paragraphs.summary: Applicant raises issues of ineffective representation, bias, procedural fairness breach, and decision reasonableness.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness issues reviewed on correctness standard; merits reviewed on reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: The procedural fairness issues raised are considered on a standard of correctness (Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 34). The merits of the Officer’s decision is reviewed on the standard of reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 16-17 [Vavilov]).

paragraphs.summary: Court states procedural fairness issues reviewed for correctness; merits reviewed for reasonableness.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh alleges incompetence of former representative Mr. D caused Officer’s decision.
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh alleges that the incompetence of his former representative, Mr. D, led to the Officer’s decision.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh relies on his affidavit, spouse’s affidavit, and response to Procedural Fairness Letter by Mr. D.
propositions.quote: In support of this allegation, Mr. Singh relies upon his own Affidavit; an Affidavit from his spouse, Ms. Davidson; and the response to the Procedural Fairness Letter submitted to the Officer by Mr. D.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant alleges incompetence of representative Mr. D, relying on affidavits and response to Procedural Fairness Letter.

propositions.text: Mr. D was served with application materials and responded through counsel on June 27, 2024.
propositions.quote: As required under paragraph 48 of the Federal Court’s Amended Consolidated Practice Guidelines for Citizenship, Immigration, and Refugee Protection Proceedings dated June 20, 2025, Mr. D was served with the Applicant’s application materials and responded to the allegations against him through his legal counsel on June 27, 2024.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. D served with materials and responded through counsel June 27, 2024.

propositions.text: Legal test for incompetence of counsel requires acts constituting incompetence, miscarriage of justice, and notice/opportunity to respond.
propositions.quote: The legal test to establish incompetence of counsel is outlined in Sidhu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 56 at para 19 as follows: 1. The representative’s alleged acts or omissions constituted incompetence; 2. There was a miscarriage in justice in the sense that, but for the alleged conduct, there is a reasonable probability that the result of the original hearing would have been different; and 3. The representative was given notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond.

paragraphs.summary: Legal test for counsel incompetence requires incompetence, miscarriage of justice, and notice/opportunity to respond, per Sidhu.

propositions.text: Applicant alleges Mr. D did not forward interview email until day before April 28, 2024, 4:40 pm.
propositions.quote: One of the alleged acts of “incompetence” raised by the Applicant is that Mr. D did not forward him the email about the interview until the day before, April 28, 2024, at 4:40 pm.

propositions.text: Applicant asserts insufficient time to prepare for interview.
propositions.quote: Further, I also do not accept the Applicant’s assertion that they did not have sufficient time to “prepare” for the interview.

propositions.text: No documents confirm late email; even if true, no incompetence as couple had enough notice and no prejudice.
propositions.quote: Despite this claim, the Applicant has not provided any documents (such as the email from Mr. D) to confirm this. However, even if I accept the Applicant only received notification of the interview the night before, I fail to see how this amounts to incompetence. The Applicant and his spouse had enough notice that they attended the interview, so no prejudice arose.

propositions.text: No acceptance that insufficient preparation time claim is valid; preparation for genuineness interview is unclear.
propositions.quote: Further, I also do not accept the Applicant’s assertion that they did not have sufficient time to “prepare” for the interview. It is difficult to conceive of what kind of preparation would be necessary for an interview that was intended to assess the “genuineness” of their relationship.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant alleges late interview email and insufficient preparation time; court finds no incompetence or prejudice.

propositions.text: Applicant claims Mr. D failed to provide copy of spousal sponsorship application despite requests.
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh also claims that Mr. D failed to provide him with a copy of his spousal sponsorship application, despite his requests for a copy.

propositions.text: Applicant suggests seeing application would have revealed omissions of addresses and US asylum claims.
propositions.quote: Presumably he is suggesting that, had he seen the application, he would have noted the omissions of his previous addresses and his failed US asylum claims.

propositions.text: No supporting documentation confirms Applicant requested application copy from Mr. D.
propositions.quote: However, the Applicant has provided no supporting documentation (such as emails or phone logs) to confirm that he requested Mr. D to provide a copy of the application.

propositions.text: Even if Applicant did not receive application, failure to correct record at interview is unexplained by this.
propositions.quote: Regardless, even if the Applicant had not received the completed application through some miscommunication on the part of Mr. D, that does not account for the Applicant’s failure to correct the record during his in-person interview on April 29, 2024.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant claims Mr. D withheld application copy; court finds no proof and unexplained failure to correct record at interview.

propositions.text: Mr. D denies incompetence allegations and denies Mr. Singh disclosed previous addresses or US visa rejections.
propositions.quote: In his response, Mr. D himself denies the allegations of “incompetence”. He specifically denies Mr. Singh disclosing to him his previous addresses or US visa rejections.

propositions.text: Mr. D provided handwritten document from Mr. Singh with address history excluding other addresses.
propositions.quote: Mr. D provided a handwritten document that he says Mr. Singh gave to him with his full address history, which does not include the other addresses.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. D denies incompetence and non-disclosure, provides handwritten address history excluding omitted addresses.

propositions.text: Mr. D claims Mr. Singh threatened him and instructed preparation of Procedural Fairness Letter response.
propositions.quote: Most disturbing is that Mr. D claims that Mr. Singh threatened him with violence and instructed him to prepare the response to the Procedural Fairness Letter, in which Mr. D states that the failure to disclose the prior US visa refusals was “due to a clerical mistake” on his part.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. D claims Mr. Singh threatened him and directed response to Procedural Fairness Letter.

propositions.text: Concerns about reliability of Mr. Singh’s affidavit due to personal interest and lack of corroboration.
propositions.quote: On balance, I have concerns with the reliability of Mr. Singh’s affidavit evidence on this issue. He obviously has a significant personal interest in this matter and his Affidavit fails to contain any corroboration.

propositions.text: Evidence from interested witness requires corroboration to have probative value (Ferguson v Canada).
propositions.quote: Evidence tendered by a witness with a personal interest in a matter typically requires corroboration to have probative value (Ferguson v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 1067 at para 27).

propositions.text: No weight given to incompetence allegations in Mr. Singh’s affidavit.
propositions.quote: As such, I would give no weight to the allegations of incompetence in Mr. Singh’s Affidavit.

paragraphs.summary: Court doubts Mr. Singh’s affidavit reliability due to personal interest and lack of corroboration, gives no weight to incompetence allegations.

propositions.text: Concerns with Ms. Davidson’s affidavit: no personal knowledge of submission, lack of knowledge at interview, limited extrinsic evidence, personal interest.
propositions.quote: I also have concerns with Ms. Davidson’s Affidavit. First, she does not state how she has personal knowledge that Mr. Singh submitted this material. She does not state that she reviewed the information submitted by Mr. Singh or was present when Mr. Singh met his immigration consultant. Second, Ms. Davidson lacked knowledge of Mr. Singh’s history during the interview. For example, she did not know who his current employer was. It is unlikely that she would know Mr. Singh’s past well enough to state that he submitted all relevant information. Finally, like Mr. Singh, there is limited extrinsic evidence supporting her claims and she also has a personal interest in the outcome of this application.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Ms. Davidson’s affidavit unreliable due to lack of personal knowledge, limited evidence, and personal interest.

propositions.text: Applicant has not established incompetent representation by Mr. D; Mr. D’s claim of threats undermines Applicant’s evidence.
propositions.quote: Upon consideration of the Applicant’s evidence, the Applicant has not established any acts or omissions that constitute incompetent representation on the part of Mr. D. I will go further and say that Mr. D’s claim that he was threatened by Mr. Singh is very troubling and it renders the Applicant’s evidence on this issue wholly unreliable.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes no incompetent representation by Mr. D; Mr. D’s threat claim makes Applicant’s evidence unreliable.

propositions.text: The Officer demonstrated reasonable apprehension of bias due to harsh questions and quick decision after Procedural Fairness Letter response
propositions.quote: The Applicant claims that the Officer demonstrated a reasonable apprehension of bias because the questions during the interview were harsh and rude, and a decision was rendered shortly after the response to the Procedural Fairness Letter.

propositions.text: These factors indicate prejudgment or bias by the Officer
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that these factors are indicative of prejudgment or bias.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant claims the Officer showed bias due to harsh interview questions and quick decision after Procedural Fairness Letter response.

propositions.text: Test for reasonable apprehension of bias is what an informed person would realistically conclude about fairness of decision
propositions.quote: The test for a reasonable apprehension of bias is outlined in Committee for Justice and Liberty et al v National Energy Board et al, [1978] 1 SCR 369 at p 394 as follows: …what would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically—and having thought the matter through—conclude.

propositions.text: Would an informed person think Mr. Crowe would not decide fairly, consciously or unconsciously
propositions.quote: Would he think that it is more likely than not that Mr. Crowe, whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly.

paragraphs.summary: The test for reasonable apprehension of bias is what an informed person would conclude about fairness of decision.

propositions.text: Apprehension of bias claims must be supported by material evidence showing conduct below standard
propositions.quote: A claim of apprehension of bias is serious and “must be supported by material evidence demonstrating conduct that derogates from the standard” (Arthur v Canada (Attorney General), 2001 FCA 223 at para 8).

paragraphs.summary: Claims of apprehension of bias require material evidence showing conduct below standard.

propositions.text: Applicant's evidence for bias claim is his and Ms. Davidson's affidavits, which raise serious credibility concerns
propositions.quote: In this case, the Applicant’s evidence supporting the bias claim is his own Affidavit and the Affidavit of Ms. Davidson. As noted above, I have serious credibility concerns with these Affidavits.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant's affidavits supporting bias claim have serious credibility concerns, says the court.

propositions.text: Certified Tribunal Record's detailed interview notes do not support bias allegations
propositions.quote: By contrast, the Certified Tribunal Record contains detailed interview notes. My review of these notes does not support the bias allegations made by Mr. Singh and Ms. Davidson.

propositions.text: Officer's pointed and direct questions do not amount to bias
propositions.quote: The Officer’s questions were at times pointed and direct, but that does not amount to bias.

propositions.text: Officer's duty includes asking personal, uncomfortable, probing questions and reminding risks of untruthful answers
propositions.quote: Additionally it was within the Officer’s duty and mandate to ask personal, uncomfortable, and probing questions about the nature of their relationship and to remind them of the risks associated with untruthful answers.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds interview notes do not support bias; pointed questions are within Officer's duty and not bias.

propositions.text: Decision rendered shortly after Procedural Fairness Letter reply does not alone prove prejudgment or bias
propositions.quote: Finally, the fact the decision was rendered shortly after the Applicant’s reply to the Procedural Fairness Letter was provided, does not, on its own, suggest or prove prejudgment or bias.

propositions.text: Applicant points to no record or procedural evidence suggesting Officer bias
propositions.quote: Otherwise, the Applicant has not pointed to anything in the record or in the substance of the decision or the procedure followed that suggests bias on the part of the Officer.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds timing of decision does not prove bias and no other evidence suggests Officer bias.

propositions.text: Allegations without evidence insufficient to meet Applicant's burden of proof on bias claim
propositions.quote: The Applicant has not provided any evidence to establish the alleged bias, and allegations without evidence are insufficient to meet the burden on the Applicant (Barros Barros v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 9 at para 50).

paragraphs.summary: Allegations without evidence do not meet Applicant's burden to prove bias, per precedent.

propositions.text: Applicant's bias claim is unfounded
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s bias claim is unfounded.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Applicant's bias claim is unfounded.

propositions.text: Interview lacked procedural fairness because it was not recorded and Officer's notes are incomplete
propositions.quote: The Applicant also claims that the interview lacked procedural fairness because the interview was not recorded, and the only record is the Officer’s notes. He alleges the Officer’s interview notes are incomplete.

propositions.text: Relies on Canadian Union of Public Employees case that absence of transcript does not violate natural justice if record suffices
propositions.quote: He relies upon Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local 301 v Montreal (City), [1997] 1 SCR 793 at para 81, which states: In the absence of a statutory right to a recording, courts must determine whether the record before it allows it to properly dispose of the application for appeal or review.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues interview lacked fairness due to no recording and incomplete notes, citing precedent on transcripts.

propositions.text: Applicant has no statutory right to transcript and IRPA does not require one
propositions.quote: The Applicant has not demonstrated that he had any statutory right to a transcript of the interview and a transcript is not required under IRPA.

propositions.text: Court has sufficient record material to dispose of matter
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the Court has sufficient material in the record to dispose of the matter.

propositions.text: Interview notes are detailed and cover matters in GCMS notes
propositions.quote: The interview notes are detailed and cover the matters mentioned in the Global Case Management System [GCMS] notes.

propositions.text: Notes suffice to dispose of bias claim given only contrary evidence are affidavits with credibility issues
propositions.quote: They are sufficiently fulsome to dispose of Mr. Singh’s claim that the Officer is biased, especially considering that the only contrary evidence is the allegations in Mr. Singh’s and Ms. Davidson’s Affidavits.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no statutory right to transcript; notes and record suffice to dispose of bias claim despite affidavits.

propositions.text: Applicant had a fair process
propositions.quote: The Applicant had a fair process.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes the Applicant had a fair process.

propositions.text: Officer's finding that marriage was not genuine is unreasonable and overlooked overwhelming evidence
propositions.quote: The Applicant also attacks the reasonableness of the Officer’s finding that the marriage was not genuine. He argues that the Officer overlooked overwhelming evidence of the genuineness of the relationship, including a marriage registration certificate, personal communications, and photographic evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer unreasonably found marriage not genuine, overlooking strong evidence.

propositions.text: Officer listed 15 reasons for doubting marriage genuineness based on inconsistencies in couple's answers and evidence
propositions.quote: The GCMS notes detail 15 reasons why the Officer was not satisfied that the marriage was genuine.

propositions.text: Couple gave conflicting information showing limited knowledge of each other
propositions.quote: The couple provided conflicting information that demonstrated limited knowledge of each other.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh said he never asked about wife's education; she said she told him many times
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh stated that he never asked about his wife’s educational history, but she stated that she told him many times.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh explained lack of knowledge by disinterest, unease, poor English
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh claimed that this was due to a lack of knowledge or interest in education programs, unease while being interviewed, and poor English.

propositions.text: Officer noted Mr. Singh and Officer understood each other; Mr. Singh showed no unease or interpreter request
propositions.quote: However, the Officer noted that he and Mr. Singh could understand each other, Mr. Singh showed no uneasiness, and Mr. Singh never requested an interpreter.

propositions.text: Discrepancy on first meeting duration: Mr. Singh said 1 hour at Starbucks; Ms. Davidson said 15 minutes
propositions.quote: Regarding their first meeting on December 19, 2022, Mr. Singh stated that they stayed at Starbuck’s for an hour. Ms. Davidson said it was for no more than 15 minutes, because she had to return to work from her break.

propositions.text: Discrepancy on wedding friends present: Mr. Singh said 2 friends; Ms. Davidson said 3 friends
propositions.quote: At their wedding, Mr. Singh claimed to have 2 friends present. Ms. Davidson said Mr. Singh had 3 friends.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh's friend Dheeraj denied attending wedding when contacted by Officer
propositions.quote: When the Officer contacted Dheeraj, Dheeraj said he was not present.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh's friend Harpreet gave inconsistent address information when questioned
propositions.quote: When the Officer called Mr. Singh’s friend, Harpreet, and asked what Mr. Singh’s current address was, Harpreet began to say 100 Yellow Brick Road in Brampton, but changed it to Toronto.

propositions.text: Officer found evidence Mr. Singh still lived in Brampton from phone, letter, and email
propositions.quote: The Officer checked Mr. Singh’s phone at the interview and found further evidence that Mr. Singh still lived in Brampton, including a letter dated March 4, 2024, and an email that Mr. Singh sent to Canada Border Services Agency on February 1, 2024, requesting that his passport be sent to the Brampton address.

propositions.text: Couple said they call daily but no call logs exist between them
propositions.quote: The couple indicated that they call each other daily, but there were no call logs between them.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh misspelled Ms. Davidson's name with a 'C' instead of 'K'
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh misspelled Ms. Davidson’s name, spelling it with a “C” rather than a “K”.

propositions.text: Discrepancy on last intercourse date: Mr. Singh said Saturday; Ms. Davidson said Thursday; interview was Monday
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh stated the last time they had intercourse was Saturday. Ms. Davidson said it was Thursday. The interview took place on a Monday.

propositions.text: Ms. Davidson could not tell Officer about Mr. Singh's current job
propositions.quote: Ms. Davidson was unable to tell the Officer about Mr. Singh’s current job.

propositions.text: Discrepancy on number of meetings before wedding: Mr. Singh said 5-6; Ms. Davidson said 9
propositions.quote: Between their first meeting and the date of the wedding, Mr. Singh said they met 5-6 times. Ms. Davidson said they met 9 times.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh often sleeps in truck in Brampton between shifts, raising cohabitation issues
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh stated that he often sleeps in his truck in Brampton between shifts, which raised serious issues about them cohabiting.

propositions.text: At interview end, Officer told Mr. Singh consequences of refusal; Mr. Singh worried about leaving Canada and packing, not about spouse or relationship
propositions.quote: At the conclusion of the interview, the Officer told Mr. Singh about the consequences of a refusal of his application. Mr. Singh expressed concerns about having to leave Canada and packing his belongings, but did not express concern about the impact on his spouse or their relationship.

propositions.text: Gap in text communications from Nov 7, 2023 to Feb 5, 2024; communications only about meetings or sponsorship application; no shared life evidence
propositions.quote: There was a gap in their text communications between November 7, 2023 and February 5, 2024. All communications were about arranging meetings or the application for spousal sponsorship of Mr. Singh. No evidence of shared activities, life, or a

paragraphs.summary: Officer found 15 reasons from inconsistencies and evidence to doubt marriage genuineness, including conflicting answers and lack of shared life evidence.

propositions.text: Inconsistent answers gave Officer ample evidence to conclude marriage was not genuine
propositions.quote: In my view, the inconsistent answers to the questions provided the Officer more than ample evidence to conclude that the marriage was not genuine.

propositions.text: Officer's finding that marriage was not genuine is not unreasonable
propositions.quote: There is nothing unreasonable about the Officer’s finding.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer reasonably concluded marriage was not genuine based on inconsistent answers.

propositions.text: Officer's finding of misrepresentation is unintelligible
propositions.quote: Mr. Singh also argues that the Officer’s finding of misrepresentation is unintelligible.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer's misrepresentation finding is unintelligible.

propositions.text: Officer explained misrepresentation materiality as omission could induce error in IRPA administration
propositions.quote: The GCMS notes provide the Officer’s rationale for finding Mr. Singh’s misrepresentation material: …Having proper and truthful background and personal information on the application is a preeminent part of the admissibility assessment. Had this information not been discovered, it could have induced an error in the administration of the Act by giving an improper impression to the officer about PA’s [principal applicant’s] information in the application being correct and honest/truthful and could have led to an improper admissibility decision. After reviewing PA’s explanation to this specific concern, I am not satisfied that PA has not misrepresented.

paragraphs.summary: Officer explained misrepresentation was material as omission could cause error in IRPA administration.

propositions.text: Explanation suffices to show omission was material under IRPA s 40(1)(a)
propositions.quote: This explanation is sufficient to explain why the omission was material. An omission is material if it relates “to a relevant matter that induces or could induce an error in the administration of [IRPA]” (IRPA ss 40(1)(a)).

propositions.text: Officer articulates why misrepresentations could lead to error in IRPA administration
propositions.quote: The Officer articulates why Mr. Singh’s misrepresentations could have led to an error in the administration of IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer's explanation sufficient to show omission was material and could cause error under IRPA.

propositions.text: Cases cited by Mr. Singh differ factually as they involved disclosure of refused visas but lack of details
propositions.quote: The cases relied upon by Mr. Singh (Alves v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 716 at paras 19-20; Koo v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 931) are factually different. In those cases, there was a disclosure of refused visas but a lack of details.

propositions.text: Mr. Singh indicated never refused admission, thus failed to disclose
propositions.quote: In contrast, Mr. Singh indicated that he had never been refused admission to any country, therefore he failed to make any disclosure.

propositions.text: Failure to disclose US visa refusals found material omission in similar cases
propositions.quote: In similar cases, failure to disclose US visa refusals was found to be a material omission (Algohar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1364 at paras 22-25; Goburdhun v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 971).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's cited cases differ; failure to disclose visa refusals is material omission per precedent.

propositions.text: Officer's finding that Applicant withheld material information is reasonable and supports misrepresentation finding under IRPA
propositions.quote: The Officer’s finding that the Applicant withheld material information is reasonable and supports the finding of misrepresentation under IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer reasonably concluded Applicant withheld material information supporting misrepresentation finding.

propositions.text: Judicial review dismissed; Officer's decision reasonable and no procedural unfairness identified
propositions.quote: I am dismissing this judicial review. The Officer’s decision meets the standard of reasonableness set out in Vavilov and the Applicant has not identified any procedural unfairness.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review, finding Officer's decision reasonable and no procedural unfairness.

propositions.text: This judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: This judicial review is dismissed.

propositions.text: There is no question for certification.
propositions.quote: There is no question for certification.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review and finds there is no question for certification.
